_about: Heritage provenance per site. Every statement carries source, url and checked (date fetched). Only fields found on fetched pages are present; unknown fields are omitted.

period.text: Generally dated to the 2nd century BCE; the article notes it may have been built by Ashoka but is generally dated slightly later. Enlarged five times in later centuries.

excavations.by: Italian mission (IsIAO), led by Domenico Faccenna

records_held_by.name: National Museum of Oriental Art, Rome (part of the finds)
City Museum of Ancient Oriental Art, Turin (MAO) (part of the finds)

disputed.claim: Date of the seated Buddha statue

views.text: Van Lohuizen-de Leeuw dates the statue to the late 1st century BCE to the early 1st century.
More conservative estimates date it to the 1st-2nd century CE.
views.source: Wikipedia: Butkara Stupa (view as summarised by the article; underlying authors not named there)

period.text: Believed to have been built in the third century (the article gives no further dating detail).

excavations.by: Sir Aurel Stein (discovery; the article does not describe excavation)

conservation.status: Described as unprotected and being damaged by treasure seekers.

records_held_by.name: Swat Museum, Saidu Sharif (the objects; the article does not say where its records are kept)

conservation.status: Damaged by the 2005 Kashmir earthquake; closed in 2007 and contents moved to Taxila; a bomb exploded nearby in February 2008; 2,700 objects returned in July 2011; reopened in a new seismic-resistant building.

period.text: No date is given; the article calls it a remnant of the Buddhist era.

excavations.by: Colonel Deane and S.A. Stein (identification; no excavation described)

conservation.status: The article does not describe current condition. Its cited headlines describe decline: Dawn, 'The Swat stupa in shambles' (2002); Express Tribune, 'Crumbling heritage: Neglected monument fading into time' (2012). Not verified by us.
conservation.source: Wikipedia: Ghalegay (citing Dawn and Express Tribune)

views.text: Tradition: built by Uttarasena, an ancient king of Swat, to enshrine his share of the Buddha's relics.
Weak sourcing: the article's citations to Dawn and Express Tribune are not clearly linked to this attribution.
views.source: Wikipedia: Ghalegay (editorial note in the article's citations)

period.text: Phases from c. 1700-1400 BCE (Bronze Age) to the Shahi and Ghaznavid periods (c. 680-1100 CE); Early Kushan c. 70-200 CE; abandonment c. 400-550 CE. Dates are approximate.

excavations.by: Italian Archaeological Mission (ISMEO), founded by Giuseppe Tucci

records_held_by.name: Hindu Shahi inscription found at Barikot in the late 19th century: Lahore Museum (the article does not say where excavation finds are kept)

disputed.claim: Start of urban settlement at Bazira

views.text: Earlier accepted sequence: fortified city founded at the end of the 2nd century BCE; urban living before c. 150 BCE was not found until 2015.
Early phases are now placed from c. 600 BCE (early-historic fortified town) and c. 600-400 BCE (start of the city, Achaemenid influence).

disputed.claim: Origin and dating of the Old Apsidal Temple

views.text: First dated to c. 250 BCE under Ashoka.
Olivieri (2024): modified from an earlier, non-Buddhist shrine from the time of Alexander's 327 BCE siege.

disputed.claim: End of the Old Apsidal Temple

views.text: The December 2021 announcement places it in the third or fourth century CE.
Other sources tie abandonment to third-century earthquakes.
views.source: Wikipedia: Barikot (other sources, not named in the article's summary)

period.text: Stylistic comparison only: the article says the relief 'may be compared to 7th - 8th century Tang sculpture in central Asia'. No other date is given.
period.source: Wikipedia: Buddhist rock carving in Manglawar (citing ValleySwat and The News, 30 Nov 2007)

conservation.status: Attack with explosives in 2007 damaged the top of the head (article cites no source for this sentence). A protective coating was applied in 2012; the face was reconstructed from laser surveys and old photographs; restoration completed with some damage deliberately left visible. Restoration credited to the Italian Archaeological Mission in Swat (article cites The Express Tribune, 13 July 2018).
conservation.source: Wikipedia: Buddhist rock carving in Manglawar
